questionStem: A 57-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of gradually progressive weakness in the shoulder and hip muscles. She has hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine but is otherw ise healthy. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Neurologic examinat ion shows moderate bilatera l weakness of the deltoid, biceps, triceps, psoas, glutei, and quadr iceps muscles. The remainder of the examinat ion shows no abnormalities. Her erythrocyte sedimentat ion rate is 85 mm/h, and serum creatine kinase activity is 2456 U/L. Complete blood count and urinalysis are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Electromyograp hy and nerve conduction studies

correctExplanation: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies are used to support a diagnosis of inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis, as in this case. Polymyositis is an autoimmune condition affecting the proximal muscles. It is closely related to dermatomyositis, however, unlike dermatomyositis, it does not present with cutaneous findings. The muscular inflamma tion is characterized by endomysial COB+ inflamma tory infiltrate. This is in contrast to dermatomyositis which demonstrates a perimysial CD4+ inflammato ry infiltrate. An inflamma tory infiltrate of the muscle occurs, causing damage to the myocytes, leading to release of creatine kinase, an intracellular molecule. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is also increased, indicating the presence of inflammation. This can be used to monitor disease progress in polymyositis. Both polymyositis and dermatomyositis are characterized by several autoantibodies: positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, and anti-Mi-2. Treatment of polymyositis involves systemic steroids followed by long-term immunosuppressive therapy with medications such as methotrexate or azathioprine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Quantitative sensory testing (Choice A) is used to evaluate damage to small and large nerve endings, not primary muscle inflammation. MRI of the spinal cord (Choice C) would be beneficial in evaluating muscle weakness because of a spinal epidural abscess or tumor. While these pathologies can cause proximal muscle weakness, other symptoms such as feve r, back pain, and sensory deficits would also be seen. As polymyositis is an inflammatory myopathy with no spinal cord involvement, imaging of the spinal cord will not be helpful. Skin biopsy (Choice D) is indicated in evaluation of suspected dermatomyositis. However, this patient does not demonstrate any cutaneous findings, and thus, a skin biopsy is not warranted. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 27-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of multip le trauma sustained in a motor vehicle collision. He is initially arousable, but he is increasingly unrespons ive over the next 45 minutes. The pupil of the left eye is dilated, and there is ptosis of the left eyelid. He begins to hyperve ntilate. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: After blunt head injury, patients can present with concussion or traumatic intracranial hemorrhage such as subdu ral hematoma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or epidural hematoma. A young patient with initial normal mental status that then becomes altered or unresponsive raises suspicion for an epidural hematoma. Epidural hematoma is classically associated with trauma to the middle meningeal artery and can present with an initial lucid interva l followed by deterioration of mental status caused by arterial bleeding and hematoma expansion. Over time , patients can have symptoms of headache, vomiting , confusion, seizures, and coma. Epidural hematomas present on CT as lens-shaped, biconvex hyperdense collec tions abutting the skull. They often compress adjacent brain and are bound by dural sutures. Epidural hematoma can be complicated by increased intracranial pressure, midline shift, uncal herniation, and death. Uncal herniation involves the uncus comp ressing the midbrain, typically affecting the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve Ill), causing pupillary dilation, ptosis, and oculomotor nerve palsy. Emergent craniotomy and decompression of the epidural hematoma is often necessary.
incorrectExplanation: nd L. Alcohol withdrawal (Choice A) presents with tremulousness, nausea, vomiting, anxiety, and tongue fasciculations. Delirium tremens is a life-threatening comp lication of alcohol withdrawal that presents with severe confusion, agitation, visua l hallucinations, and autonomic instability. Aseptic meningitis (Choice B), bacterial meningitis (Choice C), and viral meningitis (Choice L) typically present with fever, headache, and nucha l rigidity. This patient has no signs of meningitis and his altered menta l status is more likely because of blunt head trauma. Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning (Choice D) occurs as a consequence of inhaling the gas. CO has an affinity for hemog lobin that is hundreds of times greater than that of oxygen, readily displacing oxygen from heme. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, loss of consciousness, dizziness, vomiting, and fatigue. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 32-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of progressive sensory loss. Initially, only her feet felt numb, but the loss of sensation has slowly ascended symmetrica lly to the umbilicus. She also has had urinary urgency and freque ncy, nocturia, and the perception of a tight band-like sensation around her midabdom inal region. Examination shows slowing of left eye adduction during saccad ic movement of the eyes to the right. There is diffuse hyperref lexia. Sensation to pinprick is decreased to the level of the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Multiple sclerosis, the most prevalent immune-mediated demyelinating disease, may present initially with transverse myelitis though can also demonstrate neurologic symptoms from lesions in other central nervous system (CNS) locations. Transverse myelitis refers to inflammation that extends transversely across the spinal cord, leading to bilateral sensory, motor, or autonomic dysfunction. When sensory tracts are involved, sensory deficits are evident at a clear dermatomal level (also known as a sensory level, likely T10 in this patient) and may present as a band-like sensation at that level. Autonomic symptoms may present as urinary urgency or incontinence, bowel incontinence, or sexual dysfunction. According to the McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis diagnosis, patients must have evidence of demyelinating lesions that are separated in time and location. This evidence can be based on subjective symptoms or imaging evidence. This patient presents with evidence of lesions separated in space (a T10 spinal cord lesion, a lesion potentially affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus, several corticospinal tract lesions as evidenced by diffuse hyperreflexia). Though the patient did not experience discrete symptomatic episodes separated by time, the presence of multiple lesions in discrete locations makes multiple sclerosis the most likely diagnosis (as the other deficits likely arose at different times). MRI of the brain typically shows white matter hyperintensities in the periventricular region, cortex, subcortical region, cerebellum, or spine. Oligoclonal bands of immunoglobu lins, indicating immune overactivation, can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid but are not necessary for diagnosis. Treatment includes corticosteroids for symptomatic management of acute flares and long-term disease-modifying treatments such as interferon or monoclonal antibodies.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adrenal leukodystrophy (Choice A) is a rare X-linked peroxisomal disorder that results from the accumulation of very long fatty acid chains in various tissues. As a result of peripheral neuropathy and myelopathy, female carriers of the disorder may present with bilateral spastic paraparesis, sphincter dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, and sexual dysfunction. However, multiple sclerosis is more common, - - - - - - - - - -- - - - -- - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician 3 hours after a 5-minute episode of visual loss in her left eye. She has not had any other symptoms. She has hypertens ion and stable angina pectoris. Medications include lisinopril and metoprolol. Her pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg. Funduscopic exam ination shows no abnorma lities. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Amaurosis fugax describes brief episodes of transient, unilateral vision loss and is indicative of retinal ischemia caused by either microembolization or inflammation of the ophthalmic artery. It often precedes the onset of central retinal artery occlusion , which is considered an ophthalmic stroke. In the absence of signs and symptoms of giant cell arteritis, such as fever, chills, weight loss, temporal headache and tenderness, or jaw claudication, amaurosis fugax is most suggestive of embolic retinal ischemia and should prompt an emergent evaluation for sources of emboli. The majority of emboli to the ophthalmic vasculature originate from the carotid arteries and cardiac valves. Evaluation should include prompt carotid duplex ultrasonography, as well as echocardiography. Treatment of carotid vascular or cardiac valvular disease can prevent central retinal arterial occlusion, which may cause irreversib le blindness.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Complete blood count (Choice A) and measurement of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Choice B) are useful for the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis, which often presents with amaurosis fugax, thrombocytosis, and an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate. However, this patient's lack of other symptoms renders carotid arterial disease, rather than giant cell arteritis, as the more likely cause of her amaurosis fugax. Visual field testing (Choice C) may be useful for the diagnosis of glaucoma or cortical vision loss. Delaying the search for embolic sources while pursuing other diagnostic tests puts the patient at risk for ischemic stroke and blindness. MRI of the brain (Choice D) may be useful for the diagnosis of optic neuritis. It is not useful for identifying the source of emboli that are causing this patient's amaurosis fugax. Vision loss secondary to optic neuritis typically lasts for several days or weeks, rather than minutes. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 20-year-o ld college student comes to the physician for a follow-up examination 2 days after sustaining a head injury when he ran into another player while playing flag football. He did not lose consciousness but does not remember anything from the rest of the game. He was evaluated in the emergency department 1 hour after the injury; a CT scan of the head showed no abnorma lities and he was discharged. Today, he reports a mild, persistent headache that improves with acetaminophen. He has not had nausea, vomiting, or memory problems and was able to return to school today. Examination shows no abnormalities. He asks about playing i11 a flag football playoff game tomorrow. Which of the following is the most appropriate recomme ndation?

choices.A: No contact sports pending evaluation in 1 wee!<
choices.B: No contact sports pending an MRI of the brain
choices.C: No contact sports pending a lumbar puncture
choices.D: No contact sports for 1 year; schedule regular follow-up examinations
choices.E: Return to sports; no further management is indicated at this time

correctExplanation: Mild traumatic brain injury, also known as a concussion, commonly results in loss of consciousness, confusion, amnesia, headache, dizziness, nausea, or vomiting minutes after the injury. Symptoms that commonly develop within the following days include mood disturbances, photophonophobia, trouble concentrating, or insomnia. Focal neurologic symptoms, such as limb weakness or vision changes, indicate traumatic vascular injury. As such, all patients with suspected concussion should undergo a thorough neurologic examination, and a subset of at-risk patients should receive neuroimaging. All patients should be monitored closely for 24 hours for neurologic deterioration, which may indicate a developing intracranial hematoma. To prevent cumulative brain injury (eg, from a second concussion), patients with concussion should return to their usual activities in a graded fashion, beginning with the return to school or work. Each day, a more intense activity can be introduced (eg, first light aerobic exercise), culminating with contact sports after a week in uncomplicated and improving cases.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. An MRI of the brain (Choice B) may assist in detecting occult blood products in the subacute and chronic phases in patients with persistent symptoms. Repeat imaging is not necessary for patients with improving symptoms or patients in the acute phase with stable, expected symptoms such as mild headache. A lumbar puncture (Choice C) is not typically necessary for ruling out an intracranial hematoma in the setting of suspected concussion. Neuroimaging is sufficient. questionStem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after having a seizure at a dormitory party on campus. According to her boyfriend , who accompanied her, she had been drinking more water than usual and then became silent and began staring. He then witnessed her collapse to the floor and begin shaking for approximate ly 1 minute. On arrival, she is mute and unresponsive to questions. She appears restless and periodical ly grinds her teeth. Her temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows profuse diaphoresis and piloerection. Pupils are 5 mm bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnorma lities. Laboratory studies show: Prothrombin time Serum Na+ Urea nitrogen Creatinine ALT Creatine kinase 16 sec 114m Eq/L 40 mg/dL 2 mg/dL 90 U/L 1200 U/L The most likely diagnosis is intoxication with which of the following substances?
correctExplanation: 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MOMA), called ecstasy or "Molly," is a psychotherapeutic agent and drug of abuse. It is a stimulant and causes feelings of increased energy, euphoria, and disinhibition. Minor characteristic side effects include agitation, bruxism (grinding teeth), diaphoresis, and blurry vision. However, serious side effects also accompany ecstasy use. Autonomic instability (hypertension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia) can lead to life-threatening cardiovascular toxicity. This patient demonstrates another serious complication: hyponatremia secondary to increased water intake and secretion of anti-diuretic hormone. Severe hyponatremia may be accompanied by seizures, as seen in this case, as well as confusion, coma, or death. This is a particular risk in young women. Treatment includes rapid administration of hypertonic saline if recurrent seizure activity occurs, followed by gradual correction of sodium and management of autonomic instability.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 77-year-old man with hyperte nsion comes to the physician for a routine follow-up examination. He feels well. His only medication is a diuretic. His blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. On neurologic examination, cranial nerves are intact. Muscle tone and strength are normal. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the ankles but otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Measureme nt of urine lead concentration

correctExplanation: A thorough neurologic examination should include evaluation of the cranial nerves, gait, coordination, movement, muscle strength and tone, light touch, pain and temperature sensation, deep tendon reflexes, and the plantar response (Babinski sign). Deep tendon reflexes can be checked over the biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, knee, and Achilles tendons using a reflex hammer. They are graded on a scale of Oto 4 where 0 is absent, 2 is normal, and 4 is clonus (continual contraction). Reflex strength should be compared on either side and within the same patient. The Achilles reflex test is particular ly useful for evaluating pathology of the S1 nerve root and differentiating upper from lower motor neuron dysfunction. However, bilaterally absent Achilles reflex is also a normal variation, the proportion of which increases with age. Thus, in this case, the absence of both Achilles reflexes does not require any additional management. Educational Objectives: A, B, C, and D. Measurement of urine lead concentration (Choice A) is appropriate when lead poisoning is suspected. Symptoms of lead poisoning occur within days or weeks of exposure and include distal motor neuropathy. While this does cause hyporeflexia, it would affect all the reflexes in the body, not just the Achilles. It would also cause other lower motor neuron symptoms such as muscle weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations, which this patient lacks. MRI of the lumbar spine (Choice B) would be beneficia l in evaluating hyporeflexia because of a spinal nerve or spinal cord lesion. Neither of these pathologies would present with bilaterally absent Achilles reflexes alone without other symptoms like back pain or muscle weakness. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies (Choice C) are used to support a diagnosis of inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis or dermatomyositis. This condition is associated with muscle weakness, not periphera l neuropathy. These studies are not necessary in this asymptomatic individual. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause .... https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK

questionStem: A 12-year-old girl with systemic lupus erythematosus is brought to the emergency department by her parents after they had difficulty awakening her this morning. She has needed constant stimulation to stay awake. Over the past 2 days, she has had a flu-like illness and vomiting. She has been unable to take her corticosteroid and antihypertensive medications. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 60/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 180/130 mm Hg. She is obtunded but moves all extremities to painful stimuli. Funduscopic exam ination shows bilatera l papilledema with flame hemorrhages. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk and symmetric. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm/h. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy is a known complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and results from acute and severe increases in blood pressure. It may manifest with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure, and can progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical hypertension or from hypertensive retinopathy, manifesting as papilledema and flame hemorrhages on fundoscopic examination. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops, which can cause cerebral or cardiac ischemia. In genera l, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradual correction over the next day or more. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodi lator and is a preferred agent because of its short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Brain neoplasm (Choice A) can cause altered mental status in a subacute or chronic time course. It would be less likely in this patient who is presenting with acute hypertensive encephalopathy. Cerebral vasculitis (Choice B) as a manifestation of SLE is rare. Cerebral vasculitis can present with neurologic deficits, headache, seizures, or coma. Hypertensive encephalopathy is more likely in this patient. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice D) presents common ly in younger, overweight fema les taking vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol. It is usually associated with a holocephalic headache and blurry vision. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 3-day history of increased drowsiness. During this period, she also has been feeding poorly and "spitting up" after each feeding. She has not had fever. She was born at term following an uncompl icated pregnancy and delivery. On arrival, she is respons ive to tactile stimuli. She is at the 25th percenti le for length and weight and 90th percenti le for head circumference. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a bulging anterior fontanel. There is a hyperpigmented macule with hair growth on the upper lumbar spine; her parents report that this finding was noted at birth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Chiari malformations are rare congenita l malformations that typical ly present in infancy with feeding and breathing problems, spina bifida (classically manifesting as myelomeningocele), and obstructive hydrocephalus (presenting as large head circumference and bulging anterior fontane l in this patient) as a result of the downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis and tonsils. This patient's hyperpigmented macule with hair growth on the upper lumbar spine likely represents spina bifida occulta (a small defect in the vertebrae). Some patients also demonstrate eye movement abnormalities. Some Chiari malformations present in adolescence with bilateral cranial nerve palsies, weakness, and cerebellar dysfunction as a result of the downward displacement of the cerebel lar tonsils and consequent brainstem compression. Imaging typically demonstrates downward displacement of the cerebe llar vermis and tonsils, along with ventriculomegaly from hydrocephalus. Treatment involves surgical intervention for neural tube defects, shunting for hydrocephalus, and medical management of feeding and respiratory difficulties.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bacterial meningitis (Choice A) typica lly presents with fever and signs of meningeal irritation (nausea, irritability, confusion, anorexia, headache, and nuchal rigidity). Spina bifida occulta is not associated with acute bacterial meningitis. Hydrocephalus may result from bacterial meningitis. Idiopathic increased intracrania l pressure (Choice C) would present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (nausea, vomiting, positional headache) without hydrocephalus or other central nervous system pathology. Spina bifida occulta would be atypical. - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: Over the past year, a 72-year-old man has had progressive aching in his lower extremities when he walks in the shopp ing mall. Initial ly, the pain began after 15 minutes of walking and resolved after he stopped; now, it starts after 5 or 10 minutes of walking, and it occas ionally occurs when he stands up after sleeping all night. The pain radiates from his buttocks to his feet. He desc ribes it as a "terrib le" pain. He has mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but cont inues to smoke one pack of cigarettes daily. He has cervical arthritis and often has neck and arm pain. Exam ination shows decreased breath sounds bilatera lly. Strength and sensation are normal in the extremities. Babinski's sign is absent bilatera lly. Deep tendo n reflexes are 1 + in both knees and ankles and 2+ in the upper extremities. Dorsalis ped is pulses are norma l. Wh ich of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.G: Epidura l metastatic carc inoma P) Sensorimotor periphera l neuropathy
choices.H: Epste in-Barr virus infection Q) Spinal cord compression

correctExplanation: Lumbar spinal stenosis refers to the narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal, which results in compression of the lumbar nerve roots or spinal cord. Patients may present with symptoms of radicu lopathy, including back pain that radiates to the buttocks and legs, leg numbness, paresthesia, or weakness. Hip extension increases pressure on the nerve roots, while flexion of the hips relieves pressure. Consequently, patients may demonstrate neurogenic claudication, in which extension of the hips (eg, standing or walking) leads to symptoms. The most common cause of lumbar spinal stenosis is degenerative joint disease and osteophytosis, which often occurs with age. The diagnosis is confirmed by MRI. Treatment involves nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, physical therapy, and surgery.
incorrectExplanation: , M, N, 0, P, and Q. Alcohol rhabdomyolysis (Choice A) refers to muscle necrosis from long-term alcohol use. Alcohol rhabdomyolysis wou ld present with diffuse pain. Amyotrophic latera l sclerosis (Choice B) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder featuring a combination of upper and lower motor neuron weakness patterns. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 4-mo nth histo ry of increas ing low back pain that is most severe on awakening in the morning. His pain is relieved by stretching. There is no history of trauma. He is otherwise healthy except for occasional dysuria. Exam ination shows decreased forward flexion of the spine and tenderness over the lumbosac ral area and at the insertion site of the Achilles tendon. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ankylosing spondyl itis (AS) refers to an inflammatory arthritis of the spine and other joints (eg, the sacroiliac joints) along with extra-articu lar inflammation. Patients typically present at younger than age 40 years with insidious chronic low back pain that worsens at night and improves with activity (caused by the mobilization of inflammatory materia l from joints). This pattern of pain is known as inflammatory back pain. Sacroi liac arthritis and enthesitis (inflammation of the attachments of tendons and ligaments to bone) are other common joint manifestations. Extra-articular manifestations commonly include anterior uveitis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowe l disease. AS is associated with reactive arthritis, which classical ly presents with post-infectious conjunctivitis, arthritis, and urethritis. Over time, patients with AS can develop decreased spine mobility, hyperkyphosis, osteopenia, and an increased risk for vertebra l fragility fractures. Laboratory studies demonstrate increased acute phase reactant concentrations (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation rate) along with a positive HLA-B27 test in many patients. Plain x-rays may illustrate fused vertebrae and sacroiliac joints. Treatment typica lly begins with nonsteroida l anti-inf lammatory drugs and escalates to disease-modifying immunomodulating medication in refractory cases.
incorrectExplanation: nd L. Abdominal aortic aneurysm (Choice A) refers to a dilation of the abdomina l aorta, which typical ly presents with indolent abdominal pain though may present with back pain. lschemia (Choice E) has been proposed as a mechanism to explain chronic low back pain. However, the back pain would not present in the inflammatory pattern characteristic of AS. Herniated disc at L4-L5 (Choice C) and lumbar spinal stenosis (Choice F) compress the spina l nerve roots, leading to back pain and paresthesia, numbness, pain, and/or weakness of the lower extremities. Degenerative changes at the facet joints and consequent slippage of a vertebral body, known as spondylo listhesis (Choice K), is a common cause of lumbar spinal stenosis. questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 6-week history of progressive cognitive changes and "twitching movements" of his arms and legs . He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within norma l limits. Exam ination shows mild ataxic dysarthria. Muscle strength is 5/5 throughout. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ thro ughout. He has an ataxic gait and frequent irregular jerks of the upper and lower extremities. On menta l status examination , he is alert but distractible. His Mini-Me ntal State Exam ination score is 19/30. A lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows: Glucose Total protein WBC RBC 80 mg/dl 45 mg/dl none none An MRI of the brain shows vague areas of abnormal T2 signa l in the basal ganglia; these areas have no mass effect and do not enhance. Additiona l CSF analysis is most likely to show which of the following abnormalities?

choices.C: Positive herpes simplex polymerase chain react ion test

correctExplanation: This patient's signs and symptoms of rapidly progressive deme ntia, myoclonus, and ataxia are consistent with a diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a neurodegenerative prion disorder characterized by the accumulation of misfolded proteins. CJD common ly develops sporadically but may be inherited or acquired through transmissible prion particles. In prion disorders, misfolded proteins induce the misfolding of normal, native proteins, leading to a rapid intracel lular accumulation of the misfolded variant and to neuronal cell death. CJD produces spongiform encephalopathy identifiable as neuronal vacuolization on brain biopsy, along with MRI signal abnorma lities typically in the basal gang lia. CSF typical ly contains an increased concentration of 14-3-3 protein. CJD is uniformly fatal and most patients die within 1 year of symptom onset. Incorrec t Answers: A, C, D, and E. questionStem: A 47-yea r-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of gradual hearing loss in the left ear. She also has had difficulty maintaining her balance over the past 3 months. Six months ago, she had an episode of nephrolithiasis complicated by a severe urinary tract infection requiring intravenous antibiotic therapy. Examination shows a decrease of the left nasolab ial fold and a slight perioral droop when she smiles. The forehead movements are intact bilaterally. Her gait is normal, but she has difficulty with tandem walking. Audiomet ry shows moderate high-frequency hearing loss on the left with impaired speech discrimination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient most likely has an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) compressing the vestibulocochlear nerve and the upper motor neurons that synapse on the facial nerve. Acoustic neuromas are benign tumors consisting of Schwann cells that arise from the vestibu locochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII). Lesions of the vestibulocochlear nerve typically disrupt ipsilateral hearing and the sensation of head and body position, which leads to difficulty with balance and tandem (heel-to-toe) gait as in this patient. Mass effect from progressive ly enlarging acoustic neuromas can compress the neighboring facial nerve or the upper motor neurons synapsing on the facial nerve, leading to a flattened nasolabial fold and perioral droop. If the upper motor neurons are affected, the forehead is spared, as the facial nerve nucleus that controls forehead musculature is dually innervated by upper motor neurons from bilateral precentral gyri. Because of this, the patient would be expected to symmetrically raise her eyebrows. Alternatively, lesions involving the lower motor neurons of facial expression (eg, facial nerve inflammation in Bell palsy) affect the forehead and lower face together. Depending on patient age, tumor size, and symptom burden, acoustic neuromas can be managed with observation, radiation, or surgery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aminoglycoside ototoxicity (Choice B) can damage the cochlea or the vestibular organs. However, facial nerve palsy and the onset of vestibular symptoms months after aminoglycoside exposure would be atypical. Brain stem infarction (Choice C) could lead to variable cranial nerve dysfunction. However, the onset would be acute and the cranial nerve deficits would occur simultaneously. This patient instead ,experienced slowly progressive cranial nerve dysfunction over months. Mastoiditis (Choice D) refers to an infection of the mastoid air cells in the mastoid bone, typically resulting from middle ear infection in children and presenting with acute ear pain and postauricular tenderness. questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 4 ?-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of progressively severe bifrontal headac he. He has a scant beard and a sallow, waxy comp lexion. Exam ination shows bilateral tem poral hemia nopia. Visua l acuity is norma l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient's findings of headache and bitemporal hemianopsia are consistent with a diagnosis of pituitary adenoma. Benign adenomas are the most common neoplasms identified in the pituitary gland, and may secrete hormones, such as prolactin or growth hormone, causing symptoms of hyperpituitarism. More common ly, pituitary mass lesions do not cause hyperpituitarism but instead cause compression of normal pituitary neurons, leading to hypopituitarism and dysfunction of multiple endocrine axes. The pituitary gland rests in the bony sella turcica, just inferior to the optic chiasm. Retinal gang lion cell fibers from the nasal retina, which supply the temporal visual fields, decussate at the chiasm, and are vulnerable to compression by pituitary mass lesions. Since the decussating nasal retinal fibers carry information from the temporal visual fields, the resultant visual field deficit is most commonly a bitemporal hemianopsia, a finding suggestive of a pituitary mass.
incorrectExplanation: nd K. Cluster headaches (Choice A) present with severe, stabbing unilateral periorbital or fronta l pain, and are typica lly accompanied by signs and symptoms of ipsilateral dysautonomia, including lacrimation, conjunctiva! injection, and rhinorrhea. Cluster headaches do not typical ly produce visua l field deficits. Craniopharyngioma (Choice B) is a rare pituitary mass derived from remnants of the Rathke pouch that may present with bitemporal hemianopsia. However, it is more common in children. Pituitary adenoma is a more likely diagnosis in a previous ly healthy adult. Medulloblastoma (Choice C) is a common malignancy of the brain in children. It is an aggressive malignancy and produces signs and symptoms of headache, nausea and vomiting, and ocular symptoms of bilatera l abducens nerve palsy and papil ledema secondary to increased intracranial pressure. ~~. - ·- .. -. - - - ....... - - . ··-•- ·- . -• •- -· ·- ••- . - -· . . - - - . . - .. . ·••-. . - .. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening excess ive daytime sleepiness, even during important events such as meetings at work. She says she has trouble sustain ing her attention and that her symptoms are beginning to impair her work productivity. She also reports occasional episodes in which her muscles go limp and she falls sudden ly. She has injured herself during two of these episodes. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her pulse is 85/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
correctExplanation: Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep disorder characterized by daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis that responds to modafinil therapy. Narcolepsy arises from deficient production of orexins in the hypothalamus, which may result from genetic or autoimmune causes. Orexins typica lly induce the secretion of monoamines such as norepinephrine throughout the brain to promote wakefulness. As a result, patients suddenly and inappropriate ly transition into sleep during the day. Further, rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep features (eg, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis) occur during wakefulness. Cataplexy refers to a sudden loss of muscle tone and usually occurs in response to positive emotion. The clinical diagnosis should be confirmed by a polysomnography (to confirm the rapid transition into REM sleep and rule out other causes of daytime sleepiness) and a multiple sleep latency test (to confirm decreased sleep latency). Treatment includes a regular sleep schedule, avoidance of daytime naps, and, in patients with severe daytime sleepiness, modafinil. Modafinil has an unclear mechanism of action that involves increasing orexin and monoamine availability.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Weight loss program (Choice A), continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) (Choice B), and uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (Choice F) all target obstructive sleep apnea. Obstructive sleep apnea features repetitive obstruction of the pharyngeal airway during sleep and typica lly occurs in older, male patients with obesity as a result of a combination of structura l, vascular, and neuromuscular factors. Patients become hypoxemic several times nightly and experience fragmented sleep, leading to daytime sleepiness. REM sleep phenomena during wakefulness is instead consistent with narco lepsy. questionStem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents after the Thanksgiving holiday break because of a 4-day history of rapid, irregular involuntary movements of her face, trunk, and extremities. Her parents say that during this period, she has been anxious and irritable and has had headaches. She seems to be worry ing obsessive ly about things that formerly would not have worried her. She has no history of serious illness except for migratory joint pain that occurred in the early fall. Examination shows restless-appearing, genera lized involuntary movements of the face, trunk, and extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

choices.A: Autoimmune disorder of the basal ganglia

correctExplanation: This patient likely has Sydenham chorea, which is a manifestation of an autoimmune disorder of the basal ganglia. The combination of choreiform movements and migratory joint pain suggest a diagnosis of rheumatic fever, a complication of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) infection. Though arthritis is typically an early manifestation of acute rheumatic fever, Sydenham chorea is a latent manifestation and may occur months after the initial streptococcal infection. In acute rheumatic fever, streptococca l infection causes immune cross-reactivity with neurona l and cardiac cell membrane proteins and the deposition of immune complexes in the joints and soft tissues. The binding of antibodies to basal ganglia neurons results in choreiform movements (involuntary, random, irregular movements) of the face, trunk, and extremities that may be more prominent on one side of the body. Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as emotional !ability and obsessive-compulsive disorder (a disorder associated with basal ganglia pathology) may also occur. Sydenham chorea may occur as an isolated manifestation of acute rheumatic fever or in conjunction with arthritis, carditis, erythema marginatum, and/or subcutaneous nodules. As such, patients with Sydenham chorea should receive an echocardiography to evaluate for carditis. The treatment of acute rheumatic fever involves nonsteroida l anti-inf lammatory drugs and penicillin to ensure the eradication of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). Sydenham chorea is typical ly self-limited, but severe and impairing neuropsychiatric symptoms may be managed with antipsychotic or anticonvulsant medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Conversion disorder (Choice B), or functional neurologic disorder, involves acute neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not fully explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. This patient's symptoms and physical examination findings are instead consistent with a known disease. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman with breast cancer metastatic to bone is brought to the emergency department because of a 12-hour history of severe pelvic pain and numbness. She has not urinated for more than 24 hours. Her only medication is hydrocodo ne. On arrival, her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 152/70 mm Hg. Rectal examination shows decreased rectal sphincter tone. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the lower extremities. Sensation to light touch is decreased in a saddle distribution. Abdomina l examination shows suprapubic fullness. Placement of a urinary catheter yields 800 ml of clear yellow urine and resolves the pelvic pain but not the numbness. An MRI of the spine shows a tumor pushing into the L4-S 1 intrathecal space. Which of the following is the most appropr iate immediate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome occurs because of compression of the spinal nerve roots comprising the cauda equina. Often, such compression occurs as a result of malignancy, trauma (eg, compression fractures with fragment retropulsion), disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidural abscess, or spinal epidura l or subdural hematoma. Symptoms include lower extremity numbness, weakness, paralysis, hyporeflexia, perinea! anesthesia, fecal incontinence with poor rectal tone, and overflow incontinence marked by inability to void and urinary retention. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome, and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression. Initial treatment for patients with epidural spinal cord compression and neurologic deficits include symptomatic treatment, pain control, and glucocorticoid therapy prior to operative therapy. High-dose glucocorticoid therapy (eg, dexamethasone) is helpful as a bridge to definitive therapy, can help control pain, and may transient ly improve neurologic function secondary to decreasing edema at the site of cord compression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Oral administration of high-dose ibuprofen (Choice A) may be helpful for pain control, but many patients may require opioid analgesics to control severe pain. In a patient who takes hydrocodone and is opiate-tolerant, pain control will likely require opioid analgesics. Intravenous or intrathecal administration of chemotherapy (Choices C and D) or radiation therapy (Choice E) may all be helpful for definitive treatment of the tumor, but glucocorticoids are the next immediate step in management. Radiation therapy can help with expeditious local control of spinal metastases. Chemotherapy can be helpful for tumors causing cauda equina, however, systemic chemotherapy may take days to weeks to take effect. questionStem: A previous ly healthy 57-year-o ld man comes for a follow-up examination because of progress ive weakness of his arms and legs. Six months ago, examination showed no abnorma lities except for 4/5 muscle strength in all extrem ities. Current examinat ion shows fascicu lations in the hands and right lower extremity and pseudobu lbar palsy. Sensat ion is normal and cranial nerves are intact. He is oriented, and affect is appropriate. An MRI of the brain shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's disease?

choices.D: Neoplastic infiltration of the central nervous system
choices.F: Neuronal loss in the substantia nigra

correctExplanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder arising in midlife that affects both lower motor neurons arising from the anterior horn and upper motor neurons of the lateral corticospinal tract within the brain and spinal cord. Neurons degenerate because of an unknown etiology that may involve RNA processing and/or excitotoxicity, and gliosis results. Patient presentations are variable, though typically feature a combination of upper motor neuron (eg, increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron findings (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy) in an asymmetric distribution that may include the bulbar muscles. Some patients may experience cognitive or behavioral changes, though other patients are cognitively normal. The diagnosis is primarily clinical but may be supported by electromyographic findings of acute and chronic denervation and reinnervation. MRI of the brain and spine should be performed to rule out other diseases. Treatment should include riluzole, which may modestly improve survival but does not cure the disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Amyloid deposition (Choice A) occurs in Alzheimer disease. Alzheimer disease may feature apraxia (potentially related to parietal cortex damage) but does not typically lead to upper neuron or lower motor neuron dysfunction. Demyelination (Choice B) occurs in acute conditions such as pontine myelinolysis and chronic autoimmune disorders such as multiple sclerosis. Demyelination can affect the white matter of the corticospinal tract but would not affect the anterior horns (gray matter). Neoplastic infiltration of the central nervous system (Choice D) may lead to localized upper motor neuron dysfunction because of mass effect. However, generalized dysfunction in both an upper and lower motor neuron pattern is more consistent with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 3-year history of progressive forgetfulness. He has difficulty remembering names, especia lly of people he has recently met. He retired from his profession as a retail clerk 12 weeks ago because he had been forgetting the names of customers and new products and could no longer effectively perform his job. He also has had progressive difficulty with activities of daily living; his wife now chooses his clothes for him. He has no history o1f head trauma. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examination shows no abnorma lities. On mental status examination, he has an indifferent mood and affect. He is oriented to person, place, and time but takes a few minutes before he correctly names the date. His Mini-Menta l State Examination score is 22/30. There is no evidence of auditory or visua l hallucinations. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Administration of a drug from which of the following classes is most appropriate for this patient?
correctExplanation: Alzheimer dementia (AD) results from decreased cholinergic signaling and is treated with acetylcho linesterase inhibitors. Cholinergic neurons-which primarily originate from the locus coeruleus and basal forebrain and project widely to areas including the cortex­ mediate attention, learning, and memory. AD is the most prevalent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment and decline in visuospatial abilities and progresses to apraxia, language abnormalities, and dysexecutive syndrome (resulting in the inability to pick out clothes in this patient). The disease culminates in behaviora l and personality changes that prevent the patient from performing basic activities of daily living, such as bathing. Acetylcholinesterase normally hydrolyzes acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. Donepezil and other cholinesterase inhibitors non-competitively and reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity and thereby increase the amount of synaptic acetylcholine available for neurotransmission. Though donepezil may slow the rate of cognitive decline and modestly improve functiona lity, donepezil and the other cholinesterase inhibitors are not curative.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dopamine agonists (Choice B) increase dopamine signaling and therefore relieve parkinsonism. This patient does not demonstrate motor findings typical of Parkinson disease such as tremor, bradykinesia, or postural instability. NMDA receptor agonists (Choice C), such as endogenous glutamate, mediate activity-dependent synaptic changes of learning and memory. Howeve r, NMDA agonism is not a known drug mechanism because of the risk for excitotoxicity. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 37-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of a 10-day history of increasingly severe headaches. The pain has been unremitt ing for the past 18 hours; he describes it as severe and pounding. His pulse is 70/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg. Examination of the face and neck shows mild swelling and a dusky reddish-purple skin color with venous distention over the head and neck; the skin color below the neck is normal. Examinat ion of the optic fundi shows papilledema. Neurologic examinat ion shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's increased intracrania l pressure?

choices.C: Obstruct ion of cerebrospina l fluid flow
choices.D: Obstruction of venous return to the heart

correctExplanation: Obstruction of venous return to the heart through the superior vena cava (SVC) leads to superior vena cava syndrome, which presents with facial swelling, headaches, and occasional ly altered mental status or respiratory distress. Superior vena cava syndrome is most common ly caused by extrinsic compression of the SVC by an intrathoracic malignancy, such as lung cancer or lymphoma. Physical examination typically shows facial plethora, venous distension over the head and neck, and papilledema, as in this patient. While a chest x-ray may be abnormal, CT venography is typically diagnostic. Stent placement and radiation therapy are used to treat symptoms, but superior vena cava syndrome is classically associated with a poor prognosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dilation of cerebral arteries (Choice A) is associated with the development of migraine headaches, which present with unilateral, pounding-type headaches that are associated with photophobia and phonophobia. They typically last for less than 48 to 72 hours and may have a preceding aura. They do not cause facial plethora and venous distension. An intracrania l mass lesion (Choice B) classically presents with focal neurologic deficits, such as hemiplegia, altered mental status, and signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as headache and nausea. Physical examination may demonstrate papilledema. However, it would not be expected to cause discoloration of the face or venous distension of the head and neck. Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow (Choice C) and overproduction of cerebrospinal fluid (Choice E) can both lead to hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus commonly presents with headache, altered mental status or behavior, and nausea or vomiting because of increased intracranial pressure. While papilledema may be present, venous distension would not be. - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - -- - - - - -- -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

His postoperative course had been complicated by temperatures to 37.8°C (100°F) and nocturnal agitation since day 2; he has required haloperidol therapy (2 mg nightly). He has a history of bipolar disorde r. Medications include morphine by patient-controlled analgesia pump, lithium carbonate, and clonazepam. He is lying expression less in a pool of sweat and is drooling. His temperature is 40.6°C (105°F), pulse is 140/min, and blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. Examination shows wet skin and dry mucosa. There is a herpetic lesion on his lower lip. The neck is supple and the intraveno us catheter insertion site is nontender with no erythema. Bowel sounds are hyperactive; there is no organomega ly. The wound is clean and dry with no erythema. Neurologic examination shows a masked facies and a marked intention tremor. Deep tendon reflexes are hyperactive and symmetric. Babinski sign is absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is most likely in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication. NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity or tremor, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 4 ?-year-o ld man is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of progressive weakness. He says that during this period, his feet "flop" while walking, and he trips when walking up stairs. During the past week , he has had difficulty standing up from low chairs and open ing jars. He has not had pain or tingling. He has had constipation but no changes in bladder or sexual functio n. He has not had any recent infections or vaccinations. He takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He drinks three to four beers daily; for the past 6 weeks he has been drinking home-d istilled whiskey. Examination shows atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the hands and feet. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the wrist and finger extensors, interosseous, iliopsoas, and hamstring muscles and 3/5 in the anterior tibialis, peronei, and posterior tibial is muscles. Deep te ndon reflexes are 1 + diffuse ly. Babinski sign is absent. Sensory examination shows no abnorma lities. Laboratory studies show microcytic anemia and hyperuricemia . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's neurologic symptoms?
correctExplanation: Symptoms of acute lead poisoning occur within days or weeks of exposure and include abdominal pain, constipation, arthra lgia, myalgias, muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, headache, and difficulty concent rating. With prolonged exposure, chronic neurologic symptoms such as decline in cognition, depression, distal motor neuropathy, decreased hearing, tremor, and decreased brain volume on imaging may be present. The distal motor neuropathy causes lower motor neuron signs such as atrophy of muscles and hyporeflexia, as shown in this patient. Microcytic anemia is also common, since lead inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and o-ALA dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. In adults, exposure to lead primarily comes through occupation and/or hobbies. Individuals working with batteries, mining, construction , or ammunition are at higher risk. Illegally distilling alcohol has a risk for lead toxicity because of the leaching of lead from solder in the still, which is likely where this patient received exposure. Diagnosis is suspected based on exposure and symptoms and confirmed with increased serum lead concentration. Management of lead poisoning depends on the blood lead concen tration and presence of symptoms, and includes chelation with dimercaprol, ethylene diamine tetraacetate, or succimer. Sources of lead should be investigated and eliminated.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acute intermittent porphyria (Choice A) is an autosoma l dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase, resulting in deficient synthesis of heme and accumulation of porphobilinogen. Patients typically present during an acute attack with psychosis, abdominal pain, muscle weakness, neuropathy, and burgundy-colored urine. This patient's subacute presentation in the context of alcohol distillation is more consistent with lead poisoning. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: An 18-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he fell 25 feet. On examination, he is paraplegic and has urinary incontinence . Examination of the lower extremities shows absent reflexes and flaccid tone. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. X-rays of the spine show a fracture dislocat ion of T10. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's urinary incontinence?

choices.B: Compression of the S3-4 nerve roots
choices.C: Compression of the T10- 11 nerve roots
choices.D: Compression of the thoracic spinal cord

correctExplanation: An injury at the level of the thoracic spinal cord would affect the thoracic cord and may also affect segments distal to the level of the injury, including the lumbosacral segments that innervate lower extremity musculature and sensation. An injury at the level of T10 can affect sympathetic efferent fibers that provide inhibitory input to the bladder and urethra via the hypogastric nerve. Sympathetic stimulation through these fibers usually causes relaxation of bladder musculature and contraction of urethra l sphincter, resulting in urinary retention. Injury to these fibers will cause urinary incontinence as a result of impaired inhibition of bladder contraction. Spina l cord pathologies that result in urinary incontinence result in complex interactions between signals from the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and somatic nervous systems and may present with urge or overflow incontinence, altogether termed neurogenic bladder.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Compression of the conus medullaris (Choice A) often occurs at the level of L2. It can also present with sphincter dysfunction, spastic or flaccid paralysis, as well as saddle anesthesia. An injury at T10 would be unlikely to affect the conus medullaris. Compression of the S3-4 nerve roots (Choice B) describes cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina syndrome presents with low back pain, weakness of lower extremities, bladder and rectal sphincter paralysis leading to urinary retention, and sensory deficits. Compression of the T10-11 nerve roots (Choice C) would result in a thoracic radiculopathy in a dermatomal distribution resulting in pain and numbness around the umbilicus. Rupture of the bladder neck (Choice E) would present with hematuria, pelvic pain, lower abdominal pain, and difficulty voiding. It would be unlikely to be the cause of the patient's urinary incontinence and would not present with lower extremity neurologic symptoms. questionStem: Four days after admission to the hospital for intravenous antibiotic therapy for a leg rash, a 77-year-old man is unable to urinate. The rash developed 10 days ago on his right foot and has now spread to his calf. On admission, the right lower extremity was warm and erythematous. Yesterday, he had the onset of neck pain. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus currently treated with glyburide. He appears acutely ill. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). Examination shows nuchal rigidity. The right lower extremity is warm and erythematous. Muscle strength is full in the proximal upper extremities and is 4/5 in the hands. He is unable to lift the lower extremities against gravity. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. Sensation to pinprick is decreased below C?. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: An epidural abscess is a localized collection of pus in the epidural space between the dura mater and periosteum. It most commonly occurs in the spine but may occur in the brain. Most patients are elderly and have a history of concomitant infection and often have a history of immunocompromise (eg, diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, alcohol use disorder). Epidural abscess is more common in patients with a history of intravenous drug use. Infectious organisms usually spread to the epidural space hematogenously, from spinal surgery, or from adjacent osteomyelitis. Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent causative organism, but fungal infections also occur. Patients present with signs and symptoms of fever, altered mental status, meningismus, localized back pain and tenderness to palpation, and weakness, numbness, and paralysis below the affected spinal level. Treatment is with broad spectrum antibiotics and surgical drainage of the abscess.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Herniated cervical disc (Choice B) is caused by dislocation of the nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus of a cervical intervertebra l disc and may produce cervical radiculopathy or spinal cord compression. Patients present with neck pain and dermatomal arm pain and weakness. Infected hematoma of the spine (Choice C) may rarely occur following epidural hematoma formation in the spinal column. Patients often have a history of anticoagulation or coagulopathy plus immunocompromise or recent instrumentation. Meningitis (Choice D) may result from meningeal bacterial, viral, or fungal infection, and presents with feve r, meningismus and altered mental status. It is less likely to produce focal neurologic defects such as the lower extremity weakness and reduced pinprick noted in - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 23-year-o ld woman with sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department after becoming obtunded; she has a 2-day history of cough and fever. Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. She appears stuporous. She is intubated and mechanica lly ventilated. There is m1oderate nuchal rigidity. Right basilar crackles are heard on auscultat ion. Hematocrit is 21 % with many nucleated erythrocytes , and leukocyte count is 24,000/ mm 3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Transf usion of 3 units of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: Bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status, typical ly following a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms, although it can also be concomitant with another infection. Physical examination may disclose a present Kernig or Brudzinski sign, indicative of meningeal irritation, and can also demonstrate focal neurologica l symptoms or signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as hemiparesis or abducens nerve palsy. Petechiae may be present. Laboratory evaluation will show leukocytosis, and coagulation studies can show signs of disseminated intravascular coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia, decreased fibrinogen, and increased d-dimer, depending on the specific pathogen. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation is the initial diagnostic step and will reveal an increased opening pressure, increased leukocyte count with prominent neutrophi ls, increased protein concentration, and decreased glucose concentration. Culture of the CSF is utilized to diagnose the specific bacteria l cause and to distinguish between viral and fungal meningitides, or alternative diagnoses. The most common causes of bacterial meningitis in patients with asplenia, whether functiona l or operative, are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Treatment involves immediate antibiotic therapy, accompanied by glucocorticoids.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Administration of dopamine (Choice B) is utilized in the treatment of cardiogenic shock and advanced heart failure, as well as septic shock in rare circumstances. This patient is likely septic, given her tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, and leukocytosis. She is mildly hypotensive, and administration of intravenous fluids and antibiotics is the most important immediate therapy. Norepinephrine is a more appropriate initial vasopressor used to treat septic shock. CT scan of the head (Choice C) may be utilized in the evaluation of bacterial meningitis. It is commonly done prior to a lumbar puncture for CSF analysis in patients with signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as seizure, decreased level of consciousness, focal neurologic deficits, or papilledema. questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man who is HIV positive is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 1-month history of forgetfulness and inappropriate behavior. He also has been buying numerous items from the Internet. He also has had diarrhea. During the past year, he has been noncompl iant with his antiretroviral medication regimen and has had a 16-kg (35-lb) weight loss. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 46 kg (101 lb); BMI is 15 kg/m2. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows thrush. On mental status examination, he has a labile affect. He recalls zero of three objects after 5 minutes. A CT scan of the head shows prominent atrophy of the cortex and demyelination in the subcortica l white matter. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a life-threatening demyelinating disease that occurs as a result of the reactivation of human polyomavirus 2 (former ly JC virus) in patients who are immunocompromised. Most people experience an asymptomatic infection with human polyomavirus 2 during childhood, at which point the virus becomes latent. In severely immunocompromised patients, human polyomavirus 2 can reactivate and infect oligodendrocytes, leading to demyelination. Patients typically present with the subacute onset of focal neurologic deficits related to the affected brain area and cognitive impairment. Patients who are immunocompromised enough to have PML may also present with symptoms of other opportunistic infections. This patient's thrush and potential Mycobacterium avium complex infection (which likely explains his fever, diarrhea, and weight loss) indicate severe immune compromise in the setting of decreased adherence to antiretroviral therapy. MRI may demonstrate unilateral or bilateral white matter lesions without mass effect indicative of demyelination, which may progress to cortical atrophy. Lumbar puncture and cerebrospina l fluid analysis confirm the diagnosis. Treatment requires restarting antiretroviral therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Central nervous system lymphoma (Choice A), or primary CNS lymphoma, is a rare variant of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that occurs most common ly in immunocompromised patients. Typical presentation includes focal neurological deficits, neuropsychiatric symptoms, or signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, positional headache, nausea, vomiting). MRI typically demonstrates a solitary mass lesion but can reveal multiple periventricular white matter mass lesions. Primary CNS lymphoma lesions do not involve demyelination and are more likely to produce a mass effect than PML lesions. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice B) results from decreased cholinergic signaling in the cortex and basal forebrain. questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician 2 hours after the sudden onset of dim vision in her right eye.
